newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Coy Jospin keeps world waiting for policy clues.
newsitem.headline: Coy Jospin keeps world waiting for policy clues.

text.p: Newly-elected French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin made his first appearance on the world stage on Friday but the bookish Socialist leader made no policy statement, telling reporters he was too new to the job.

Greeted by delegates with a standing ovation on arrival at the European Social Democratic Parties' Congress on Thursday, he embraced party loyalists, posed for a photograph with a young woman admirer and shook hands wherever they were proffered but had little to say to the reporters dogging his every step.

"I've just arrived (in office). I'm starting to go through the papers. I will not speak on questions of substance here today," he told journalists after delivering a keynote speech which largely echoed the addresses of fellow European left and centre leaders.
Like other speakers, he focused on the need to fight unemployment, encourage economic growth and foster equality among citizens of the European Union (EU).

He said that his government would remain faithful to its election manifesto but later brushed off questions about a pledge to renegotiate the EU's stability pact, meant to limit member states' budget deficits after the planned launch of the euro currency in 1999.
"On the stability pact, I have no comment," he said.
One theme he did stress was that, while the ideal was to build a united Europe, the individual sovereign state was the building block.
"Europe cannot replace nations," he said. "Nation states remain the historic centre of democracy."
He welcomed Labour's landslide victory in the May 1 British elections and said that together with his own win it offered a chance to build a new Europe.

Jospin met British Prime Minister Tony Blair on Thursday but said nothing about the content of the discussions other than that they had talked of the emotional effects of their respective wins and to compliment the British leader on his French.
"He speaks French better than I speak English," said Jospin, who spoke clearly in English several times during his visit

Asked about the crucial relationship with German Christian Democrat Chancellor Helmut Kohl, whom he will meet at a Franco-German summit next week, Jospin said that their ideological differences posed no difficulties.
"I have a great deal of respect for Chancellor Kohl. There are no problems," he said.
